# Entuned

> Original music for multi-location retail stores, measured against the same operational data retailers already use for everything else. Not licensed catalog. Not a playlist service.

Entuned makes original music for retail environments and works with multi-location lifestyle retailers on pilot deployments that produce measurable outcomes against their existing analytics data.

The category we operate in sits between the traditional in-store music business (Mood Media, Soundtrack Your Brand, SiriusXM Business, Cloud Cover) and the retail analytics business (RetailNext, Sensormatic, Standard AI). Those two categories have never shared data. That gap is where audio fails to show up as a measured variable in retail performance.

## Research Foundation

Four decades of peer-reviewed research on music and consumer behavior sit behind the category. Milliman (1982) established that tempo changes shopper pace and spending. Areni and Kim (1993) showed classical music in a wine shop moved customers toward more expensive bottles. Yalch and Spangenberg (2000) documented that familiar music shortens visits. These findings have been replicated across retail formats and decades.

- [What to Ask Your Music Vendor at the Next QBR](https://entuned.co/blog/qbr-questions-music-vendor.html): Ten questions a VP of Retail Ops should put to the music vendor at the next quarterly review. Half of them will not have answers. That is the information you need.
- [Tuesday vs. Saturday Traffic: What Your Data Actually Says](https://entuned.co/blog/tuesday-vs-saturday-traffic.html): The two days look like different stores. They often are. What the Tuesday-Saturday gap reveals about your customer mix and what to do about it.
- [Mall vs. Street: Making the Same Brand Feel Right in Both](https://entuned.co/blog/mall-vs-street-location.html): The same merchandise, the same signage, and a completely different customer. What multi-location operators get wrong about keeping brand coherence across formats.
- [Your Music Is Already Talking to Your Customers. The Question Is What It's Saying.](https://entuned.co/blog/music-already-talking-to-customers.html): How in-store music sets the customer's emotional register before your sales associate says a word — and which playlist staples are actively working against your floor team.
- [The Composer Who Wanted You to Ignore Him](https://entuned.co/blog/the-composer-who-wanted-you-to-ignore-him.html): Erik Satie invented furniture music in 1917 and discovered the central problem of background music on his first public performance: people don't respond to music the way you design them to.
- [The Organ in the Department Store](https://entuned.co/blog/the-organ-in-the-department-store.html): John Wanamaker built the world's largest pipe organ into his Philadelphia department store in 1911 and played it twice a day for over a century. He understood that sound shapes a retail space. He just had no way to measure it.
- [The General and the Wire](https://entuned.co/blog/the-general-and-the-wire.html): Muzak was the first company to treat background music as a controlled variable with a measurable outcome. The instinct was right. The connection between music and outcome never actually closed.
- [Turning On the Radio](https://entuned.co/blog/turning-on-the-radio.html): When shop owners turned off Muzak and flipped on the radio, they traded one problem for another — free music with someone else's ads, opinions, and a DJ who'd never walked their floor.
- [The Pianist in the Store](https://entuned.co/blog/the-pianist-in-the-store.html): Nordstrom's live pianists were the only retail music system that adapted to the room in real time. By 2020, the last one was gone — and with him, that capability entirely.
- [The Supermarket Study](https://entuned.co/blog/the-supermarket-study.html): Ronald Milliman proved in 1982 that slow-tempo music increases retail spending by 38%. Over 600 citations. Almost no implementation. Entuned controls 31 variables where Milliman measured one.
- [The Wine Aisle](https://entuned.co/blog/the-wine-aisle.html): A 1999 study proved French music sold French wine and German music sold German wine — and the shoppers had no idea the music was influencing them. This is associative priming, Layer 3 in Entuned's model.
- [The Nightclub on the Sales Floor](https://entuned.co/blog/the-nightclub-on-the-sales-floor.html): Abercrombie & Fitch ran stores at 90 decibels as a deliberate demographic filter. Every store's music selects for an audience — most retailers just aren't doing it on purpose.
- [The Sound of Nothing](https://entuned.co/blog/the-sound-of-nothing.html): Costco doesn't play music and it's a deliberate brand choice. Most retail silence is just neglect. Every store has a soundscape whether it programmed one or not.
- ['Tis the Season (For the Same 40 Songs)](https://entuned.co/blog/tis-the-season.html): Holiday music creates a saturation problem for retail staff that nobody accounts for — each song plays 136 times per season per employee. The customer hears it once. The employee lives inside it for 40 hours a week.
- [The Playlist Era and the Open Loop](https://entuned.co/blog/the-playlist-era-and-the-open-loop.html): The playlist era solved curation and licensing but never solved measurement. From Muzak's retirement in 2013 to the manager's personal Spotify account, the loop between music and outcome has been open for a century.
- [Closing the Loop](https://entuned.co/blog/closing-the-loop.html): Every era of retail music discovered that sound changes behavior and operated without connecting the music to the outcome. Entuned closes that loop with 31 Flow Factors, in-store behavioral measurement, and a compounding Specification-Outcome Map.
- [What Jazz Musicians Hear That Spotify Can't Tag](https://entuned.co/blog/what-jazz-musicians-hear.html): The gap between what a trained musician hears and what streaming metadata captures is the same gap that makes most in-store music ineffective. Harmonic density, voice leading, and rhythmic feel are the variables that move behavior — and none of them live in a tag.
- [How Your Playlist Is Tanking Retail Dwell Time](https://entuned.co/blog/bye-bye-bye-dwell-time.html): A song looped the word "leave" thirty times in a thrift store and shoppers drifted toward the exit. The mechanism doesn't care about price point. Filtering for negative lyrics won't catch most of it — tempo, harmonic density, and arrangement push people out below the level any content review would flag.
- [Cloud Cover Music: What It Costs and Why There's a Better Way](https://entuned.co/blog/cloud-cover-music.html): Cloud Cover is one of the more affordable catalog-based commercial music services at $16.95–$26.95/month per location. The licensing economics that force that monthly fee don't exist in Entuned's model — which is why Entuned's free tier is unlimited and indefinite.
- [Music for Retail Stores: How to Get It Right Without Overpaying](https://entuned.co/blog/music-for-retail-stores.html): Most retailers treat music as an afterthought — someone's phone, a random playlist, and a licensing letter that shows up later. This post covers why retail music matters more than most owners think, what's wrong with catalog-based services, and how Entuned generates original outcome-calibrated music with a free tier that runs indefinitely.
- [BMI License: What It Costs and How to Avoid Needing One](https://entuned.co/blog/bmi-license.html): Most small business owners discover public performance licensing the same way — a letter from BMI. This post explains what BMI is, what a blanket license actually costs when you add ASCAP, SESAC, and GMR, and how switching to music with no third-party rights holders eliminates the licensing obligation entirely.
- [Free Music for Retail Stores: Yes, It Actually Exists Now](https://entuned.co/blog/free-music-for-retail.html): Free in-store music wasn't possible before because the licensing economics wouldn't allow it. Entuned owns its music outright — no PRO involvement, no per-performance royalties — which is why the Entuned Free tier is genuinely free, indefinite, and unlimited.

- [Grocery Store Music: What to Play and Why It Matters](https://entuned.co/blog/grocery-store-music.html): Grocery is the retail environment where Milliman's landmark tempo-pacing research is most direct. Slower music means slower shoppers, and slower shoppers spend measurably more. This post explains the mechanism, what most grocery operators are doing wrong, and how Entuned's dwell time outcome mode applies to the category.

- [Retail Music Has a Quality Problem](https://entuned.co/blog/retail-music-quality-problem.html): The music in upmarket retail stores is getting noticeably worse — thinner, cheaper, off-brand. The reason is structural, not aesthetic: as licensing gets more expensive, traditional providers default to cheaper catalog. This post explains the licensing trap, why retailers who design every other surface still outsource their soundtrack, and what comes after better playlists.

- [You Didn't Notice the Music. That's the Point.](https://entuned.co/blog/you-didnt-notice-the-music.html): If you ran Entuned for a shift and didn't really notice the music, that's the system working as designed. Retail music is environmental design that operates on dwell, engagement, and spend whether or not anyone consciously hears it. The right metric is what moved on the floor, not whether the staff liked the songs.
